items.questionAndWhy: Does unexpected social evaluation affect momentary self-esteem differently across ages?
items.whatTheyDid: Gregorova and colleagues studied 141 people aged 10–40 using an experimental social evaluation task and repeated daily-life assessments.
items.whatTheyFound: Laboratory reactivity to unexpected feedback peaked in late adolescence. In everyday life, younger participants responded more strongly to perceived interaction pleasantness and unexpected social experiences. Individual reactivity across settings was associated. Age comparisons do not establish within-person developmental change.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX developmental research can distinguish feedback valence from the gap between expected and experienced feedback. Neither age nor feedback response alone establishes an individual's susceptibility or future behavior.
items.streamTitle: Social feedback surprises were linked to greater self-esteem reactivity in adolescence
items.streamSummary: An experiment and daily-life sampling of 141 people linked age to self-esteem responses to unexpected social feedback; the laboratory and daily-life age patterns differed.
items.attribution: Gregorova, Will, Burkard et al. — Nature Communications (November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do people who feel socially disconnected organize the same ongoing experiences into events differently?
items.whatTheyDid: Lu and colleagues analyzed two fMRI datasets (65 and 43 participants) collected during naturalistic video viewing, fitting hidden Markov models to neural event sequences.
items.whatTheyFound: Higher loneliness was associated with less similar segmentation across participants, especially in higher-order brain regions. Fit to a group-average model was poorer for some videos. The observational neural analysis cannot establish whether loneliness causes differences in interpretation or vice versa.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX sensemaking studies can test whether people identify different event boundaries despite shared exposure, using explicit behavioral descriptions alongside neural measures. Neural differences alone do not establish divergent beliefs.
items.streamTitle: Loneliness was associated with divergent neural segmentation of shared events
items.streamSummary: Two fMRI datasets linked loneliness to less shared neural event segmentation during video viewing; the direction of causality remains unknown.
items.attribution: Lu, Sava-Segal and Baek — Communications Psychology (November 26, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How much do behavioral interventions change policy support when many independent research teams test the same broad question?
items.whatTheyDid: A preregistered project assigned 19,558 US online participants to treatment or control conditions across 55 independently developed experiments, measuring stated support and design-specific behavioral proxies, often donations.
items.whatTheyFound: Pooled effects on behavioral proxies were small (d=0.06; 99.5% CI 0.001–0.124). Four of five common stated-support outcomes showed small effects; increases across outcomes were 1.7–2.4 percentage points. Researchers substantially overestimated effects. Proxies are not actual voting or policy adoption.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX intervention assessment, use multiple independently designed tests, report small and null effects, and compare expert expectations with observed outcomes. The measured effects are specific to these US carbon-pricing studies and do not establish a general persuasion rate.
items.streamTitle: Fifty-five randomized designs found small shifts in carbon-pricing support
items.streamSummary: A 19,558-person many-designs experiment found small average changes in carbon-pricing support across 55 trials, below researchers' expectations.
items.attribution: Holzknecht, Schwaiger, Blanco et al. — Nature Human Behaviour (November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Why can the population impact of a digital message differ from the effect measured among exposed individuals?
items.whatTheyDid: Tappin presented a conceptual argument and illustrative exposure-by-effect comparisons grounded in prior persuasion and digital-media research.
items.whatTheyFound: The commentary argues that reach varies more than per-person persuasive effects across content and may therefore account for more variation in aggregate impact. Its numerical illustration is not a new measured campaign outcome or a universal empirical law.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX defensive information-environment assessment, distinguish verified unique exposure, individual response and aggregate outcomes. Neither impressions alone nor experimental effect sizes alone establish actual population impact; assess uncertainty and repeated exposure.
items.streamTitle: Digital persuasion commentary distinguishes exposure from per-person effects
items.streamSummary: A conceptual commentary argues that population-level media effects depend on both reach and per-person response, and that exposure variation may dominate. It reports no new campaign trial.
items.attribution: Ben M. Tappin — Nature Human Behaviour (commentary; November 26, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can research agents advance an existing project while preserving prior requirements and respecting unfinished or outdated artifacts?
items.whatTheyDid: ARE-bench reconstructed 75 tasks from researchers' actual sessions and workspaces, covering seven research stages and 1,173 binary checklist criteria; seven models were tested.
items.whatTheyFound: The strongest model met every criterion on 66.2% of tasks. Three models passed about 69% when only delivery and general norms were checked, versus 28.4–40.0% with historical and workspace requirements included. This is a preprint benchmark, not a representative estimate for all deployments.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX can evaluate research automation against preserved decisions, file lineage and acceptance criteria as well as output quality. Use real project-state checks rather than a clean-room demonstration.
items.streamTitle: Research agents struggled to honor prior decisions in real project workspaces
items.streamSummary: ARE-bench found that judging deliverables alone substantially overstated research-agent success when historical and workspace requirements were omitted.
items.attribution: Lin, Ren, Xu et al. — arXiv preprint (November 10, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can an AI planner recognize that a request is incomplete and obtain information that actually changes the decision?
items.whatTheyDid: Ask2Decide used 43 planning tasks with missing facts whose relevance was determined by optimization solvers. Researchers collected 79 sessions from 19 people to calibrate a simulated operator and tested four LLMs.
items.whatTheyFound: Human replies after incorrect plans omitted the correcting fact 43% of the time versus 7% for an uncalibrated simulated user. Across models, initial infeasibility ranged from 58–98% with missing facts versus 5–28% with complete inputs. Agents recovered relevant facts only modestly more often than irrelevant ones. The benchmark is ongoing and uses constrained planning problems.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX decision-support tests can include missing constraints, independently check feasibility, and score whether clarification retrieves decision-relevant facts. Results are not human decision-performance estimates.
items.streamTitle: Planning agents frequently missed facts needed to construct feasible plans
items.streamSummary: Ask2Decide found large feasibility losses when AI planners lacked facts, and substantial differences between human and uncalibrated simulated operator replies.
items.attribution: Tang, Fan, Zou et al. — arXiv preprint (November 9, 2026; revised November 15)

items.questionAndWhy: Can common preprocessing and validation choices distort estimates of how accurately neural signals predict behavior or perception?
items.whatTheyDid: Wong and colleagues investigated leakage in supervised and unsupervised preprocessing, including dimensionality reduction, and analyzed cross-validation of autocorrelated neural time series.
items.whatTheyFound: Preprocessing can transfer information across train/test boundaries. Leakage sometimes reduced rather than inflated performance, while random folds could greatly inflate accuracy on autocorrelated signals. The work provides analytical explanations and recommendations; it does not establish the error rate of unrelated datasets.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX behavioral time-series models can fit preprocessing only within training partitions and compare temporally separated or participant-held-out evaluations. Transfer beyond neural decoding is a methodological hypothesis requiring dataset-specific checks.
items.streamTitle: Neural decoding methods exposed leakage from preprocessing and random time-series splits
items.streamSummary: Neural decoding analysis showed that preprocessing leakage can bias performance in either direction and random folds can overstate accuracy for dependent time series.
items.attribution: Wong, McCullough, Lu et al. — Nature Communications (November 25, 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can reusable recordings support comparisons between neural responses, broad affect dimensions and specific reported emotions during video viewing?
items.whatTheyDid: Yoo and colleagues released MEG recordings of 23 people watching 40 clips, with dimensional and discrete emotion annotations, peak-intensity segments and a separate online stimulus-validation survey of 500 people.
items.whatTheyFound: The survey supported differentiation of intended stimulus categories. The authors reported 89.87% trial-level classification accuracy for four stimulus quadrants. This measures classification of stimulus categories in the study, not reliable identification of an individual's private emotional state or independent field performance.
items.whatItMeans: PSYWERX can use the annotated stimuli and recordings for consented research comparing affect measures. Test generalization across people and videos and keep stimulus labels separate from actual individual experiences and behavioral outcomes.
items.streamTitle: Open video-emotion dataset pairs neural signals with granular human ratings
items.streamSummary: A public MEG/video dataset includes 23 recorded participants, 40 clips and survey validation in 500 respondents; reported classification concerns stimulus categories.
items.attribution: Yoo, Kim, Choi et al. — Scientific Data (November 14, 2026)
